title: 'Not impressed with the company': Flock cameras spark debate over privacy, public safety in Chelan County
byline: Kalie Worthen, The Wenatchee World, Wash.
summary: Chelan County Sheriff Mike Morrison defended the office's two-year Flock Safety ALPR pilot program at a Cashmere City Council meeting, citing investigative successes while criticizing the company itself and acknowledging vandalism of several cameras and residents' privacy concerns. The article discusses Washington's new Driver Privacy Act (SB 6002) shortening ALPR retention to 21 days and notes East Wenatchee tabled a Flock master agreement after residents raised concerns following an October 2025 revelation that Wenatchee and East Wenatchee PDs had unknowingly shared data with federal agencies including Border Patrol.

key_quotes.quote: I don't like mass surveillance and I believe Flock cameras are mass surveillance. Any time you're recording license plate numbers and interconnecting that over a large area over a long time, collecting all that data, that becomes surveillance in my opinion

Flock Safety drew statewide attention to the Wenatchee and East Wenatchee police departments in October 2025 after a University of Washington article revealed that the two departments unknowingly shared network access with the federal government, including U.S. Border Patrol, through a default setting.
East Wenatchee City Council tabled a Flock camera "master agreement" Sept. 15 after several local residents raised concerns about the technology.
The law shortens the length of time ALPR data can be stored from 30 days to 21 days, unless it is being used in an active case.
I'm not convinced that we keep this technology yet. I don't think we've had it up long enough
